query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small concentration of yttrium to the boride-based components will improve their resistance to molten‐aluminum corrosion by promoting the formation of a more adherent and protective alumina scale on the surface.
generation.material_initial_state: Standard boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment (without yttrium modification) that tend to experience corrosion from molten aluminum.
generation.intervention: Introduce a microalloying treatment or surface modification step to incorporate a controlled amount of yttrium into the boride material.
generation.conditions: Components are exposed to molten aluminum at typical hot-dip plating temperatures (around 660–750 °C) under industrial plating conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a thin, Y-stabilized Al2O3 (alumina) layer at the surface of the component.
generation.mechanism: During exposure to molten aluminum, the yttrium segregates to the surface and at grain boundaries in the boride, where it promotes the nucleation and adhesion of an alumina scale. This Y-enriched oxide barrier is less prone to spallation and slows further degradation by reducing metal–molten aluminum interdiffusion and dissolution.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated boride components, the yttrium-doped boride should show reduced corrosion effects (e.g., lower weight loss and decreased corrosion current density) under molten aluminum exposure.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics (such as weight loss and electrochemical corrosion measurements) from standard, yttrium-free boride components under molten aluminum conditions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect should persist under the temperature and exposure durations typical for hot-dip aluminum plating; however, the optimum yttrium concentration must be kept within a range that does not compromise the mechanical integrity or introduce unwanted phases. The precise concentration range remains to be fully determined.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal yttrium content and its long-term stability under thermal cycling conditions are uncertain. Moreover, the effectiveness of this intervention in a full-scale industrial setting needs additional investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical boride-based component samples: one set modified to include a controlled, small concentration of yttrium and a control set without yttrium. Subject both sets to prolonged exposure in molten aluminum under conditions mirroring typical hot-dip aluminum-plating processes (e.g., 700 °C for 100 hours).
measurements: Electrochemical corrosion (e.g., corrosion current density) measurements
Surface characterization using SEM/EDS and XRD to assess the presence and quality of the alumina layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the yttrium-modified samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (for example, less than a 10% reduction in weight loss or corrosion current density) over the unmodified samples, or if the surface analysis shows the absence or poor adhesion of a protective alumina layer, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractBoth crack-free AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and Y and Hf co-doping AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively.
